etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gulf, goulf, golf, from Old French golf, from Italian golfo, from Late Latin colfos, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “bosom, gulf”), of obscure origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelp- (“to curve, arch”).

definitions.definition: A hollow place in the earth; an abyss; a deep chasm or basin.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book III”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: He then surveyed / Hell and the gulf between.

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: Of course, there was no arguing against this, but one thing was clear, we could not attempt that leap in the dark; the only thing to do was to wait for the ray of light which pierced through the gulf at sunset.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XL, page 62:
quote.text: ⁠For though my nature rarely yields⁠To that vague fear implied in death;⁠Nor shudders at the gulfs beneath,The howlings from forgotten fields;  […]

quote.citation: 1906, Lord Dunsany [i.e., Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany], Time and the Gods‎[1], London: William Heineman, →OCLC, page 55:
quote.text: It is told that that traveller came at last to the utter End and there was a mighty gulf, and in the darkness at the bottom of the gulf one small god crept, no bigger than a hare, whose voice came crying in the cold: “I know not.” And beyond the gulf was nought, only the small god crying.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i], line 23:
quote.text: Witch's mummy, maw and gulf / Of the ravined salt sea shark,

definitions.definition: That which swallows irretrievably; a whirlpool; a sucking eddy.

quote.citation: 1864, Alfred Tennyson, “Sea Dreams”, in Enoch Arden, &c., London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, page 100:
quote.text: [T]here is no such mine, / None; but a gulf of ruin, swallowing gold, not making.

definitions.definition: (geography) A portion of an ocean or sea extending into the land; a partially landlocked sea
(mining) A large deposit of ore in a lode.
(figurative) A wide interval or gap; a separating space.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 16:26:
quote.text: Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed.

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: `Behold now, let the Dead and Living meet! Across the gulf of Time they still are one.'

definitions.definition: (figurative) A difference, especially a large difference, between groups.

quote.citation: 2012 September 7, Phil McNulty, “Moldova 0-5 England”, in BBC Sport‎[2]:
quote.text: England were graphically illustrating the huge gulf in class between the sides and it was no surprise when Lampard added the second just before the half hour. Steven Gerrard found his Liverpool team-mate Glen Johnson and Lampard arrived in the area with perfect timing to glide a header beyond Namasco.

quote.citation: 2018 May 17, “Corbynomics would change Britain—but not in the way most people think”, in The Economist‎[3]:
quote.text: Piecing together Corbynomics is difficult, not least because it has evolved during Mr Corbyn’s time in charge of Labour. The gulf between the Labour leadership’s past positions and the milder proposals in the manifesto means that enormous uncertainty hangs over what a Corbyn-led government would do in office.

quote.citation: 2022 November 4, Fiona Harvey, “UN chief warns ‘we will be doomed’ without historic climate pact”, in The Guardian‎[4]:
quote.text: Rich countries must sign a “historic pact” with the poor on the climate, or “we will be doomed”, the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, has warned, as a deepening gulf between the developed and developing world has put climate talks on the brink.

quote.citation: 2023 August 7, Nesrine Malik, “British people are kinder and less divided than politicians give us credit for”, in The Guardian‎[5]:
quote.text: The result is a widening gulf between people’s reality and what they are relentlessly told they actually believe in and care about.

definitions.definition: (Oxbridge slang) The bottom part of a list of those awarded a degree, for those who have only just passed.

quote.citation: 1852, Charles Astor Bristed, Five Years in an English University, page 205:
quote.text: Some ten or fifteen men just on the line, not enough to be plucked or good enough to be placed, are put into the "gulf," as it is popularly called (the Examiners' phrase is "Degrees allowed"), and have their degrees given to them but are not printed in the calendar, nor were they at this time allowed to try for the Classical Tripos.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto X:
quote.text: […] if with thee the roaring wells⁠Should gulf him fathom-deep in brine;⁠And hands so often clasp’d in mine,Should toss with tangle and with shells.

definitions.definition: (Oxbridge slang, transitive) To award a degree to somebody who has only just passed sufficiently.

quote.citation: 1852, Charles Astor Bristed, Five Years in an English University, pages 228–229:
quote.text: The mention of gulfed and plucked men brings me back to myself.
The good Professor scolded, predicted that they would all be either gulfed or ploughed.

quote.citation: 1876, Sir George Otto Trevelyan, The life and Letters of Lord Macaulay‎[6], volume 1, page 83:
quote.text: Everyone who knows the Senate House may anticipate the result. When the Tripos of 1822 made its appearance his name did not grace the list. In short, to use the expressive vocabulary of the university, Macaulay was gulfed:—a mishap which disabled him from contending for the Chancellor's medals, then the crowning trophies of a classical career.
